speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of Finance):
speechtext:
1.	In 1867 only Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and the Province of Canada (divided into the Provinces of Ontario and Quebec by the
B.N.A. Act of 1867) joined together to form Confederation. With the exception of Newfoundland, the other provinces did not exist as political entities at that time. The portion of the total debt of the Province of Canada attributable to each of Ontario and Quebec has not been established. The net debt of each of the three provinces on the eve of Confederation, June 30, 1867, was $9.0 million, $7.8 million and $74.4 million respectively for the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Canada.
2.	The Provincial Public Accounts show the debt of each province. However, because the provinces' accounts are not all on the same basis, these figures are not easily comparable from province to province. The latest available comparative figures can be found in the Dominion Bureau of Statistics Publication, Provincial Government Finance. As of March 31, 1965, the total direct and indirect debt, less sinking funds, for Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario respectively were approximately $330,887,000; $365,322,000; $3,145,783,000 and $3,981,994,000.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. F. Whelan (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries):

speechtext:

There was an accidental brief overflow in the new Electric Reduction Company of Canada plant during the start up, from a system containing water which may be contaminated with fluorine and phosphorus. speechtext:
On a point of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I should point out that the applause, although appreciated, is not for the same reason as that accorded to the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) a few minutes ago.
From concept to reality, the gestation period of Canada's National Library was even longer than that of medicare. Plans for a National Library were mentioned by Sir John A. Macdonald as early as 1883, but it was not until 70 years later, on January 1, 1953, that our National Library came into being. Now only 16 years old it is one of the youngest of our national institutions but already one of the most important. At a time when knowledge is multiplying at a dizzying pace, a national repository of fact and thought is assuming growing importance.
We must be certain that the legislative framework for such a vital institution does not restrain its ability to respond to current and future needs. In the 17 years since the National Library Act was first framed, the role and function of libraries have changed greatly and will be evolving rapidly in coming years.
The age of electronics is creating new opportunities for libraries to serve as complete information centres. As the key-stone of our country's library network, the National Library must be able to serve as the nerve centre of a fully integrated and highly automated information system at the disposal of the Canadian people and their institutions. The purpose of this bill is to update the charter of the National Library so it may assist Canadians to cope better with the current explosion of research and publications, which is a world phenomenon. It reflects the changes of the past 17 years in the library world and permits the National Library to assume the dynamic role required of it today. The bill also aims at avoiding costly duplication during this period of explosive library developments, while ensuring the best possible service with the human and material resources available. Automation is coming to libraries. Data banks will have to make bibliographic information available to all libraries through an inter-library communications network. Such developments are necessary, but expensive. We must ensure that they occur with adequate co-ordination so that we will get full value for our investment.
The National Library is now being asked to assist in the planning and co-ordination of
National Library Act
collections in research libraries and of electronic information retrieval systems. Two factors make such planning particularly urgent. First, considerable funds are now available to university libraries for the purchase of books, and there is wide recognition of a need for co-ordination of acquisition policies so that unnecessary duplication may be avoided. Second, the advent of electronic techniques for storing, processing and transmitting bibliographic information has had considerable impact on library methods and techniques. It has become imperative to achieve compatibility among the systems to be established by the principal libraries of Canada. The National Library of Canada must be at the very centre of our National Library network; at the same time, it is the logical instrument to co-ordinate Canadian efforts with those in other countries.
Government libraries, no less than others, can profit from co-ordination. They collectively own resources from which the entire country, as well as the government itself, can benefit. Within the government, as outside it, better co-ordination of book collections and the establishment of common services using electronic techniques should be ensured. The National Library should take the lead in developing the network of government libraries, as well as that of other research libraries in Canada.
This bill seeks to enable the National Library to fulfil its role more adequately at both the national and the international levels. Clauses 7, 8 and 9 are the key clauses in this respect. Paragraph (2) of clause 7 states:
(2) Subject to the direction of the Governor in Council, the National Librarian may co-ordinate the library services of departments, branches and agencies of the Government of Canada including
(a)	the acquisition and cataloguing of books;
(b)	the supply of professional advice, supervision and personnel; and
(c)	the provision of modern information storage and retrieval services including photocopying and microfilming services, electronic and other automated data processing services and facsimile or other communication of information services.
Clause 8 provides that the National Librari-as may enter into agreements with Canadian or foreign libraries in this respect.
In order to assist the National Librarian to carry out such a program more adequately, it was considered advisable to reorganize the National Library Advisory Council so that the National Science Library, the Library of Parliament, the Public Archives, the National Museums of Canada, the Canada Council and the Association of Universities and Colleges of

National Library Act
Canada would have ex officio representation on the council, which will be known as the advisory board. These provisions are found in Clause 9.
It is desirable that new Canadian publications be listed as soon as possible in the national bibliography, Canadiana; accordingly the time limit for deposit is being reduced from one month to one week. The present act requires the deposit of a single copy when the retail value of two copies exceeds $25. Enacted 16 years ago, this provision is no longer realistic and under clause 11 publishers would henceforth be required to deliver two copies of their books, unless the retail value of one copy exceeds $50.
Clause 15 repeals Section 52 of the Copyright Act, which calls for the deposit of two copies of a book at the time of its publication. Considering that this deposit in no way adds to the protection afforded a book through registration; that Canadian publications are deposited by virtue of the National Library Act; and that the majority of publications deposited under the Copyright Act are foreign publications which the National Library has no desire to receive systematically nor to keep permanently, it seems advisable to repeal this clause. This proposal is being made with the approval of the various agencies concerned.
I look forward, Mr. Speaker, to hearing hon. members' remarks on this subject. Detailed questions will be dealt with in the standing committee. If at that time there are proposals for amendments, I am sure the minister will be pleased to consider them.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING ADMINISTRATION, POWERS OF LIBRARIAN, ETC.
speechtext:
As
has already been indicated by the Parliamentary Secretary of the Secretary of State (Mr. Stanbury), Mr. Speaker, the moving of the motion for the second reading of Bill C-171 is an important occasion in the parliament of Canada as well as throughout the nation generally. It was in 1952 that the National Library Act was first approved by parliament. At that time it was thought that something concrete in terms of a building and facilities would be forthcoming in short order but, as already indicated, there was a long period of delay from conception through gestation until the actual library facilities became available.
While we in this parliament have the privilege of debating this important event, I do not think we should forget that many other

Canadians, inside and outside parliament, have been responsible for the achievement of the last few years in establishing this important cultural and educational facility. In particular I would like to pay tribute to a gentleman who was Dominion Archivist and National Librarian from the time the act was passed in 1952 until his retirement last fall, Dr. Kaye Lamb. He and many others, including the Canadian Library Association and L'Association Canadienne des Bibliothecaires de Langue Frangaise, have been closely associated with this project.
Then, too, Mr. Speaker, far too often when politicians leave this house they are gone and forgotten. I think we should recall that someone whom we all regret has retired, at least temporarily, from the political arena was the person who had the privilege of guiding the development of the new National Library building through its initial stages. I refer to the Hon. Davie Fulton who as minister of public works made the initial announcement that Canada would have a national library built in time for our centennial celebrations in 1967. This was one of the major projects that were designed to help Canada celebrate its centennial. Incidentally, it was one of the projects completed on time. In this respect there are others in the capital city, such as the National Centre for the Performing Arts, that have not yet been completed.
It is interesting to note that the National Library building was completed at a total cost of some $13 million, and it is not a bad building at that. I am sure the Parliamentary Secretary will agree with me in this regard, although I recall that Mr. Richard Jackson, at the time the building was first completed described it as the capital's ugly duckling. We have all sorts of architectural experts in the nation's capital who like to comment on the architectural style and achievement of individual building developments. Perhaps I might be permitted to quote from the article by Mr. Jackson in the Ottawa Journal of July 27, 1966, titled "Capital's Ugly Duckling," in which he wrote:
Well for one thing, the new library "doesn't reflect an architectural awareness of its setting."
Which means its too jammed up against Wellington Street, lacks the attractive framework that proper setting on the escarpment, overlooking the Gatineau, might have given it.
And those windows.
Like peepholes in a prison wall.
He suspects that the library's appearance was conceived to blend with, if not exactly match the two twin, veteran's and trade buildings, across Wellington.
February 24, 1969



And those, looking like something straight out of East Berlin, have been called all sorts of things. None of them flattering.
I do not know why it is that when we consider establishing cultural institutions in Canada, in particular in the nation's capital, we do not give careful consideration to the architectural style and make certain that it conforms to the high purpose of their cultural intent. But we cannot do much about it now. The buildings are there, and at least they provide the facilities that make it possible for the Parliament of Canada to re-enact the National Library Act and bring it into line with the current and expanding needs of library services in Canada.
One of the reasons for the delay from the point of conception to the point of realization was that Canada, like many other nations, had become obsessed with the achievements of the mass media as opposed to the printed word. There was a great explosion in knowledge and information immediately following world war II. It was in 1948 that the Canadian Library Association in conjunction with its French language counterpart, L'Association Canadienne des Bibliothecaires de Langue Frangaise, first approached the government of Canada with the suggestion that the time was long past when we needed a national library.
Unfortunately those earlier overtures coincided precisely with the time when we became obsessed, enchanted and almost hypnotized with the development of mass media, for that was the time when television was coming into its own. We were in the age of McLuhanism with its new gospel, "the medium is the message", and for a time we tended to forget that society as we know it today was made possible by reason of the availability of man's knowledge in the great libraries round the world. I know that Dr. Marshall McLuhan is at the moment the high priest of information, and I think we are still on the wave of McLuhanism which quite openly preaches that books are obsolete packages and that the real motivating force, from the standpoint of communication, springs from the idiot tube of the instant electronic medium of communication.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
Some one has said that this has also resulted in the creation of an instant electronic folklore which is able to generate almost over night, or at least within the space of a few days, myths that become more far-reaching and more embracing in terms of their grip on
National Library Act
the minds of the people than the actual facts underlining a social situation. Someone also has said that our neglect of books and our tendency to become overly enamoured and mesmerized by mass media is one of the main reasons we are confronted with rather disconcerting examples of the generation gap today. We find ourselves confronted with a generation that has been educated almost exclusively by watching television with the violence and other selective distortions that are possible with this instant electronic creator of mythology. The result is that we have on our hands today a generation that has been cut off at the roots, as it were, and which has no deep and abiding connection with man's historic past or man's cultural past. We have what one might call a cut flower civilization, a civilization that has cut itself off at the roots and in which there are tendencies toward anarchy and even nihilism.
I wish to say these things briefly at the second reading stage because when the bill is before the committee we will deal with the mechanics of the legislation itself. I should like to emphasize, as I did in my opening remarks, that I believe this is a major development in the Canadian body politic because it means that at long last we are recognizing the importance of the printed word in maintaining the onward march of civilization. I think the pendulum is swinging back, as it must, in the face of some of the incidents which have been all too evident in Canada in recent weeks and months. There is a recognition that if we are to build for the future we must recognize that a creative and responsible future, and the young people who will provide the leadership for that future can only emerge if the young people become saturated-I almost used the word "indoctrinated" but it has a nasty ideological tinge today-with the values, accomplishments and cultural accumulations of the past.
While attending the University of Toronto I remember taking a course on empires and communications from that very eminent scholar, Dr. Edgar Innis. The thesis of that course was simply that the quality of successive civilizations, empires, or whatever you wish to call them, was directly related to the type of communications which prevailed predominantly in any particular period of man's history. I believe there is much truth in a thesis of that kind as reflected in the type of society and type of world in which we are living at the present time.

February 24, 1989
National Library Act
Actually there is not too much to say with regard to the bill itself. I have before me the brief that was presented to the cabinet, the government and parliament by the Canadian Library Association and l'Association Cana-dienne des Bibliothecaires de Langue Fran-gaise. As I compare the brief with the bill we have before us it is evident that a good deal of the inspiration for the revision of the act came from the recommendations of the two main bodies active in the area of library development.
I notice, however, one discrepancy which I believe is of some significance. No doubt there will be some discussion about this at the committee stage when we reach that particular part of our study. The associations recommended that the National Library should be a truly national institution rather than merely another department of government. It seems to me this is in keeping with parliament's attitude toward the C.B.C. and similar activities of that kind because the C.B.C. operates in a sensitive area so far as parliamentary and political control is concerned, particularly with regard to education and dissemination of information.
We maintain the posture that the control of such agencies by parliament and the government should be minimal. We know in respect of the C.B.C that the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) is the minister responsible for reporting to parliament for that body. I think it is for this reason that the library associations have recommended that the National Library of Canada should be set up as a Crown corporation to give it as much independence of action as possible in order to remove it as far as possible from direct and immediate governmental control and also to ensure that the objectives that are of major importance to Canada may be rapidly developed. I believe that this source of information should be a truly national institution embracing all aspects of Canadianism. The government has chosen not to accept the recommendation.
As I go through the bill I find it interesting to note that there are several clauses which specifically emphasize that the government is to have the closest possible administrative control. Let me refer for a moment to clause
4.	Under the heading "Administration of Library" it states:
The Minister shall preside over and has the supervision of the management and direction of the Library.
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
This is quite different from the solution applied in the reorganization of the national museums. That bill was passed last fall. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, as will other members of the house, that a board of trustees was set up which has the immediate responsibility for administering the affairs of the national museums in Ottawa as well as branches of the national museums in other parts of Canada. I suppose this was done because of the necessity in the cultural, educational and informational field of keeping the control by the government as far away from the agencies as possible. The government has chosen not to follow the same procedure in respect of this bill. We will be very much interested in finding out the reason this course of action has been taken.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
I could refer to another clause, clause 7, which has the same sort of emphasis. Under the heading "Powers and Duties of Librarian" subsection 1 states "subject to the direction of the minister", and subsection 2 says "subject to the direction of the Governor in Council, the National Librarian may co-ordinate the library services of departments, branches and agencies", etc. So in every instance we find this strong, controlling influence to be exerted by the minister and by the Governor in council. This is a reversal of the usual formula which has applied to national educational services.
There is one other matter with which I should like to deal at this stage of our discussion. I want to pose a question, and perhaps this is not the time to do so as we will be able to deal with these matters in committee. However, I do want to give notice that members of the official opposition in probing this matter will be inquiring about the status of existing library facilities in the government service as well as in other parts of Canada.
The co-ordinating function is emphasized as one of the major purposes of the legislation. On this point a good many of the recommendations of library associations have been included in the legislation before us. Certainly the advisory board provided for by this measure is much more representative and broader than that provided under the original act of 1952 in that it includes persons such as the Parliamentary Librarian, the Dominion Archivist, the National Science Librarian and persons nominated by the National Museum
February 24, 1969

and the association of universities and colleges of Canada. It also recognizes the professional status of librarians in Canada at the present time.
I note that the brief submitted to the government recommended that there be direct representation on the advisory board from both the Canadian National Library Associations as well as its French-speaking counterpart. We shall be inquiring as to why this recommendation was not accepted.
It would seem to me that library science is still in the formative stage. We know there is a drastic shortage of qualified professional librarians, and it would seem to me that these professional associations at this stage would have a very important function on the advisory board in advising as to how all the problems of a rapidly expanding service could be handled. In addition to that problem I am wondering about our Library of Parliament. Hon. members are and have been very much concerned about the welfare of our own library during the long interregnum which has been referred to during discussions in the house, while we awaited the advent of The National Library.
The Library of Parliament has served both as the national library and the parliamentary library. As a result of this dual function members of parliament were assured exceptional service in terms of the availability of current publications. Now that the emphasis is moving somewhat from the Parliamentary Library to the National Library I trust there will be sufficient co-ordination maintained in order that both the upper and lower chambers of parliament will have ready and immediate access to the great flood of information constantly pouring forth from printing presses in this and other countries of the world. We do not want to be placed in a position where we have to depend for our sources of information on the mass media. We might become badly brainwashed if we are restricted to the impact from instant electronic communications which are so successful in perpetuating many of the emphases eating at the foundations of our society. We will, of course, pursue this when the legislation is before the committee.
I wonder too about the fate of such an outstanding library as the National Science Library. The advisory board will include the librarian of the National Science Library, but it operates under the National Research
National Library Act
Council and we must recognize that the National Library is essentially associated with the humanities and social sciences. I trust that in the gradual development and evolution of the functions of the National Library, programs will be sufficiently flexible to ensure the present high standard of our National Science Library.
I think my time has almost expired, Mr. Speaker, and before you bring me to an abrupt conclusion I shall voluntarily wind up my remarks. I have made these observations because we are moving in a slightly different direction in cultural development. We are giving close control to the government, the minister and the Governor in Council in an area of educational, informational and cultural development. This is a departure different from the government's handling of the C.B.C., the National Museum and other agencies of this kind. We will continue to prod the government in this regard before the committee to make sure there is going to be sufficient flexibility on the advisory board that we may get the best possible service from our National Library as a national institution in every sense of the word and not merely as an arm of government.

speakeroldname: Mr. H. E. Gray (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT ASSOCIATIONS ACT PERMISSION TO SOCIETY TO BECOME FEDERALLY INCORPORATED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the present Co-operative Credit Associations Act deals principally, as the house may know, with the Canadian Co-operative Credit Society, incorporated by parliament in 1953, and with those provincial central credit societies that become members of this federal society. At the present time, therefore, the provincial centrals for British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario are subject to this act.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
This act, which was passed by parliament in 1963, applies to certain parts of the cooperative credit movement in Canada. The movement is organized on three levels. At the first level are the local credit unions organized on a parish, a community, or an employment basis. They accept deposits from and make loans to their members. For the most part, members are individuals falling within the group that the local credit union is organized to serve. In some cases these credit unions may have other co-operative organizations as members as well as individuals. The local credit unions are incorporated pursuant to provincial law and are supervised by provincial authorities.
At the second level are provincial central credit unions. These organizations act as central credit unions for the local credit unions. They accept deposits from their members and make loans to them. Their members are the local credit unions and sometimes other cooperative organizations. The local credit unions rely on their deposits with the centrals as the main part of their liquidity reserve to meet demands for withdrawal of funds. The provincial central credit unions are organized under provincial law and they do not have individuals as members.
Finally, at the third level is the Canadian Co-operative Credit Society. This society is authorized to receive deposits from its members, to borrow or raise money from its members and from chartered banks, and to lend 29180-372J
DEBATES	5861
Co-operative Credit Associations Act money to its members. It also has certain investment powers. The federal society has for its members a number of provincial central credit unions and also a number of cooperative corporations carrying on business in two or more provinces. However, the act does not have any special application to these latter organizations other than indicating they are eligible for membership.
The original purpose of the federal society was to act as a central credit union for the provincial centrals, and also to some extent for the co-operative organizations doing an interprovincial business. This was to have opened the way for the exchange of funds from the co-operative movement in one region of Canada to that in another. A further purpose was to remove doubts that had been expressed about the constitutional position of the provincial centrals.
The bill before us amends certain provisions of the Co-operative Credit Associations Act. The amendments will have the effect of relaxing some of the restrictions now included in the act and granting some extensions of powers to the societies subject to it.
Over the past several years the credit union movement has asked that amendments be made to the act in order to permit the Canadian Co-operative Credit Society to be able to carry out more fully the purposes originally intended for it and to permit the provincial centrals subject to the act to continue their sound and orderly development, in the light of current conditions. The government is therefore proposing these amendments in order to meet these requests.
The main points dealt with in the bill may be outlined as follows. At present a provincial central may become a member of the Canadian Co-operative Credit Society and subject to the act only if declared eligible by parliament. It is proposed, therefore, to enable this declaration to be effected by the Governor in Council. Also, provision is made to effect amendments to the act of incorporation of the federal society by letters patent.
The federal society may now borrow money only from banks and from its own members. An amendment would broaden the borrowing powers to enable it to raise money from any source. Organizations subject to the act are at present limited to a maximum of ten times the capital, reserve and surplus in the amount of deposits they may accept or money they may borrow. An amendment would raise this limit to 20 times, subject to approval of the minister on specific application.
5862	COMMONS
Co-operative Credit Associations Act
A change would be made in the liquidity reserve requirements. At present, organizations under the act are required to maintain an amount equal to at least 5 per cent of their deposits in the form of cash and a further 15 per cent in the form of cash or government, municipal, or school securities. An amendment would delete municipal and school securities from the classes eligible to meet this reserve requirement since it is thought that municipal and school securities as a class are not always readily saleable and thus do not represent a good source of liquid funds to meet withdrawals of deposits.
Following the introduction of this measure in the other place, it has come to the government's attention that the immediate application of this change would result in undue losses to certain societies. The Goverment believes, therefore, that a transitional period should be allowed for its implementation in cases where undue losses might otherwise occur. It is proposed to suggest an amendment to this effect when this bill comes before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
The change in liquidity reserve requirements would also permit provincial centrals to count as part of their liquidity reserve deposits with the federal society. The federal society may not now lend more than 10 per cent of its capital and deposits to any one member. An amendment would permit it to exceed this subject to certain conditions. The amendment would put the federal society on the same basis as the provincial centrals in this regard.
Investment powers would be changed slightly to make it clear that provincial centrals can invest in mortgage loan companies. The co-operative movement in some provinces has formed mortgage loan companies for the purpose of financing housing for its members. This amendment would clarify the power of a credit society to make an investment in such companies.
Certain other amendments are proposed by way of clarifying provisions of the act and transferring certain responsibilities from the Treasury Board to the Minister of Finance.
The Canadian credit union movement, including the caisses populaires, serves more than five million members, or approximately a quarter of our total population. It has accumulated nearly $3.3 billion of savings. As CUNA International, a voice of the credit

DEBATES	February 24, 1969
union movement, put it in a brief to the finance committee of this house in 1967:
The credit unions and caisses populaires in Canada serve their members as non-profit service organizations, and play a vital and essential role in the economy and growth of Canada as a whole.
This government recognizes the importance of the credit union movement and is therefore presenting these amendments as a way of assisting it in carrying out this key role. The credit union movement is active in many parts of Canada including my own city of Windsor, and as someone who is himself a credit union member I am pleased to urge the house to approve this bill by way of second reading.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT ASSOCIATIONS ACT PERMISSION TO SOCIETY TO BECOME FEDERALLY INCORPORATED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems that the changes proposed by the parliamentary secretary to the Co-operative Credit Associations Act have two objectives, one of which is flexibility in changing conditions. When I look at what is to be achieved and what is the end objective of the bill, I am brought back to the considerations which I expressed at the time of the changes in the Bank Act, that more and more of these organizations such as credit unions and caisses populaires are actually carrying out banking functions. To me the amendments to this act point up the fact that we are getting a hodgepodge of legislation dealing with banking.
The other day the government house leader indicated that amendments to the Trust Companies Act and Loan Companies Act will be put before the house. There again we have concerns that are carrying on some banking functions. Therefore when we want to consider the whole Canadian banking picture we must refer to the Bank Act and to the Quebec Savings Banks Act, which banks, mind you, will revert back to the Bank Act. We must also look at the Trust Companies Act, and the Loan Companies Act, and now we have the Co-operative Credit Associations Act as well as a number of related acts.
Frankly it is my view that we would have a much sounder and saner banking picture if we described the functions of banking, and if any organization, whether provincial or federal, wishes to engage in one of the functions of banking then it must conform to that general banking act. We would have none of this nonsense of provincial governments saying that because they have incorporated a particular co-operative they control its operations in the field of money and banking.
February 24, 1969

[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
This, to me, is an indication of the need for a complete revision. We must take a careful look at this picture if we are to have a sound banking system across the country. I remember occasions when we were dealing with associations incorporated under this act-I believe the last was from Saskatchewan-and when unfortunately there were certain complexities concerning the holding of shares. I shall not go into the details, but we had a difficult time. We shall consider the amendments more closely in committee, and I trust they will serve to iron out some of these difficulties.
The first major change indicated by the parliamentary secretary has to do with an amendment to section 4 of the act so as to allow the cabinet by Order in Council to authorize the inclusion in a co-operative credit association of a credit society incorporated under provincial charter. At the present time parliament has to declare itself on such applications. The amendment does not, of course, remove this power from parliament; it gives additional power to the cabinet. The exercise of these new powers is to be founded on Orders in Council and these, of course, will be published. I hope this does not amount to an expression of the mood of the government that more and more authority should be removed from parliament and placed in the hands of the Governor in Council. I see the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair) shaking his head as though this were the one thing farthest removed from the mind of the government. Personally, I am not so naive as to take this all on trust.
We are to see a degree of flexibility introduced so that with the approval of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), which in effect means the approval of the Superintendent of Insurance, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) may alter a charter by issuing modified letters patent. I believe this is a good step to take. I do not think there is any need for the great majority of these co-operative associations to be asked to come to parliament for incorporation. The machinery within the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs should now be sophisticated enough, and its personnel sufficiently large and sophisticated in most cases, to enable these arrangements to be removed from parliament.
DEBATES	5863
Co-operative Credit Associations Act
I shall reserve my opinion with regard to some of these proposed changes, particularly those relating to the powers and ability of these associations to borrow or raise money. If we refer to the original act-and I intend to make only incidental reference to section 8-we find that in this proposed amendment we are going far beyond the provision "to borrow or raise money from its members or from an association of which it is a member or from chartered banks in Canada...*
I do not think this is the purpose of such an organization as we are considering. This proposal is simply giving more and more people an opportunity to compete for money, whether or not as a result of competition they face from trust companies and the banks at the present time, which on occasion offer what I call deceptively attractive rates of interest that the financial situation of the country does not warrant. Now it is intended to give the caisses populaires and the credit unions the same right, and I shall want to say something on that aspect of the subject during the committee hearings.
There are other proposals which we shall need to consider in detail later but, basically, with the reservations I have mentioned and one or two others, we believe that by and large this bill should receive second reading, bearing in mind that it is to be sent to the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT ASSOCIATIONS ACT PERMISSION TO SOCIETY TO BECOME FEDERALLY INCORPORATED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the members of the New Democratic Party I wish to welcome the amendments to the Co-Operative Credit Associations Act which have been placed before us by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gray). I believe this legislation represents a step forward for the credit union movement in Canada and is an indication of the growing strength of the movement and of the increasing role it is playing in the Canadian economy and in promoting the welfare of the Canadian people.
This legislation was requested by the credit union movement, I understand, and the bill now before us is supported by the interested organizations. I also understand that it has been requested for some seven or eight years, and it is regrettable it should have taken so long to bring this bill before parliament. I trust the legislation now before the house is an indication that the government intends to proceed with the long-delayed introduction of
February 24, 1969

Co-operative Credit Associations Act a federal co-operatives act, as has been announced. Account must be taken, of course, of the experience of previous years when the introduction of such a measure was also announced but was not proceeded with for one reason or another. I hope the fact that we are now proceeding to consider these amendments relating to credit unions and co-operative credit associations is an indication that at long last the government is going to proceed with the other legislation I have mentioned.
The details of the bill before us will, of course, receive further study in committee. I understand that this measure provides for greater flexibility in co-operative credit arrangements, enabling credit societies to join in the operations of the Canadian Co-operative Credit Society. I understand, also, that it extends the operating limits of participating members in ways already indicated by the parliamentary secretary.
I cannot join at this time in the reservation expressed by the hon. member for Edmonton-West (Mr. Lambert) with respect to the powers granted to the Governor in Council affecting new members coming under the scope of this legislation. I feel that adequate safeguards already exist to prevent any step being taken which is not in the public interest.
The credit union movement is playing and will continue to play a valuable and important role in the Canadian economy. In particular, it will continue to be of help to people whose financial circumstances prevent them using other financial institutions as they might otherwise wish to do. The credit union movement has developed and grown as a result of the initiative of people who joined together in voluntary co-operation to form their own organizations and develop them, often in the face of difficult obstacles. The present bill is to the credit of those who pioneered this development and carried it on to the point where the movement has become a sophisticated and mature organization on the Canadian scene. Often the progress that has been made has resulted in the face of grudging acquiescence or indifferent acknowledgement by government.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Many people owe some degree of financial stability and independence to the help given them by the credit union movement. I believe that in the future public policy needs to be geared to a greater extent to the encouragement and fostering of the growth of such

institutions. Further growth of credit unions and related institutions is needed, particularly in face of the unprecedented acceleration and spiralling of interest rates that we are witnessing today.
I note that the credit union movement has also had to increase its interest rates in spite of its desire to hold them down. The increase has been necessitated by the need to compete for savings funds which would otherwise go to other institutions that have considerably raised their rates since they are no longer restricted by law in the matter of interest rates on loans. Credit unions find it very difficult to do their job in view of the nightmare growth in interest rates that has taken place over the past two or three years and the increased cost of borrowing.
Present developments respecting interest rates, the cost of borrowing money and financing illustrate the folly of unrestricted rates. At the same time, for the many little people in Canada the credit union movement represents a small island of hope for survival from the advancing swells of uncontrolled financing costs. In this respect I welcome this legislation and I hope that in future we will see a public policy in Canada geared to a greater extent to helping movements like the credit unions to grow and prosper on the Canadian scene.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words in support of these amendments to the Co-operative Credit Associations Act. I think it is significant that in this the first session of this parliament we as members should be presented, first of all, with these important amendments to this valuable piece of legislation and, second, that we should have been advised by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) on Thursday last that it is the firm intention of the government to bring forward a major bill providing for the federal incorporation of cooperatives. These measures indicate to me not only that credit unions and co-operatives have come of age and are important but that this parliament and the people of this country recognize their importance.
It is very difficult for me to add anything of a descriptive nature to the address of the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), the parliamentary secretary, who spoke on second reading of this bill. The background of the legislation was described by him. I think it is well known by all those interested in the credit union movement that it started in
February 24, 19G9	COMMONS
various provinces of this country with the organization of local credit unions or caisses populaires. As these local units grew in importance they found it desirable and helpful to federate into provincial credit societies or organizations for a similar purpose, called credit union leagues, where their surplus funds were pooled. The aim of these organizations was to ensure that the surplus that might be on hand in one credit union at one time could be made available for lending to another credit union which might be short of funds.
As these organizations grew across the country it became apparent that the experience at the provincial level could be duplicated with profit at the federal level. This resulted in the development of a movement in the early fifties for the incorporation of a federal co-operative credit society. This legislation was passed in 1953, and in that year the first and only credit society incorporated under it, the Canadian Co-operative Credit Society, was formed. This legislation is similar in form to other financial leglislation such as the Trust Companies Act, the Loan Companies Act and similar statutes which provide a general regulatory pattern for financial institutions and also provide that they must be incorporated by a private act.
At this stage in its history I think the Canadian Co-operative Credit Society can be said to have realized some of the purposes of its founders, but not all of them. This is recognized by the members and the directors of the society. To some extent the failure of the society to realize all the hopes of those who had a hand in its organization merely recognizes the democratic and free thinking mood of the credit union movement in Canada. Not every credit union or member of a credit union thinks alike, and as a consequence this society is not supported in its membership by all credit unions in the country.
I think it is also true to say that to a very large extent the reason the Canadian Co-operative Credit Society has not realized at this stage in its history all the hopes of its founders is that it has been inhibited and restricted by the conditions set forth in the Co-operative Credit Associations Act. It is extremely fortunate that this bill is now brought forward because it reproduces, I think faithfully, the request of the Canadian Co-operative Credit Society for responsible amendments that will remove the main restrictions that have inhibited its growth and development.
DEBATES	5865
Co-operative Credit Associations Act
I do not wish to create a wrong impression when I say that the organization has not realized all the hopes of its founders, because it has made very substantial progress and represents a valuable and responsible financial arm in the total credit union movement in Canada. The assets of this organization, as disclosed by its most recent balance sheet, exceed $577,000.
Of greater significance in measuring the strength of the credit union movement is the combined strength of credit societies in the four provinces which comprise the membership of the Canadian Co-operative Credit Society. These are the British Columbia Central Credit Union, the Ontario Co-operative Credit Society, the Saskatchewan Co-operative Credit Society, and the Co-operative Credit Society of Manitoba. The annual report of the Canadian Co-operative Credit Society presented at its annual meeting on April 8, 1968, indicates the strength of these four important member credit societies and the tremendous growth which they have achieved in the past decade.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
In 1956 the combined assets of these four societies were $18,575,000. In 1966 the combined assets of these four societies had risen to $139,590,000. This is an indication of the growing strength and importance of the credit union movement in this country, to which the parliamentary secretary referred in his remarks. A total of more than $3 billion in savings are invested in credit unions. It is a matter of great significance that one of four Canadians is a member of a credit union.
I do not intend to repeat the description given by the parliamentary secretary of the proposed amendments. It would be more to the point to examine them in detail in the standing committee. But in view of the remarks made by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) it might be helpful if I were to comment on two specific proposals. The hon. member referred to the fact that it will now be possible to add members to a co-operative credit society by Order in Council. I think the hon. member reserved his decision on whether this was a prudent move. He is probably completely unaware of the fact that this change has been urgently requested by the credit union movement and by the Canadian Co-operative Credit Society.
5868	COMMONS
Co-operative Credit Associations Act
I will not go into detail as to the legal structure in the Co-operative Credit Associations Act. It is unique in the legislative history of this parliament and represents an attempt by parliament to meet possible problems of jurisdiction in a sensible fashion. This statute provides that any provincial credit society which becomes a member of any federal credit society obtains the benefits of a parallel federal incorporation and is invested with the powers and authorities of a federal credit society as well as the preexisting powers of the provincial society. Membership in a federal credit society carries with it the added status of a federal corporation.
It was the feeling of parliament in 1953 that any organization which became a member of such a society would be named in the private act. This was found to be a very onerous requirement because when a new member wished to join the credit society the private act had to be amended. The proposed change permits new members to be added under the authority of an Order in Council. This is a highly beneficial change which will be welcomed by credit unions.
Reference has also been made to the enlargement of borrowing powers of co-operative credit societies. Formerly they were restricted to borrowing from other credit soci-ties and from chartered banks. These restrictions have now been removed and this will enable the Canadian Co-operative Credit Society to borrow money more generally. Anyone familiar with the co-operative movement in this country will realize the importance of the Canadian Co-operative Credit Society having the power to raise money more generally by bonds and debentures and by the issuance of other securities. This will,
I am sure, be supported by the members of co-operative associations.
The parliamentary secretary and the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Burton) have both spoken about the importance of the credit union movement in this country. This means of extending financial services has been important to people who for one reason or another do not have ready access to the banking system and the more standardized financial institutions. It must be borne in mind that credit unions over the years have filled a gap in the existing financial institutions of this country by bringing financial services close to people who needed them. They have been instrumental in providing instruction and knowledge in economics and in the wise use of credit to their members. They have in the very best and most realistic

DEBATES	February 24, 1969
sense of the term provided for self-help among the people of this country. They have provided a realistic competitive regulator in the financial market. Parliaments should recognize the achievements of the credit union movement and not restrict its legitimate development. It should be the desire of all hon. members to encourage the development of credit unions in this country. This they can do by supporting this legislation.
Last week I attended the annual meeting of a large credit union in my constituency. It was a very happy occasion for people who had borrowed money from that financial institution. The credit union had achieved a substantial saving in the past year. The most important act of the credit union at that meeting was to pass a resolution reducing the interest paid on loans made to members by approximately one-fifth. This is reproduced all over the country time after time.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
The actions and activities of credit unions have been greatly beneficial to Canada. The support they have received and the encouragement that has been given to them by central credit societies has been important, and the most important of these central credit societies is the Canadian Co-operative Credit Society created under this statute. I think all of us can be hopeful, if these legislative changes are made, that we will make a great and significant contribution to the further development of that society and of Canadian credit unions.

Mr. Speaker, briefly I wish to endorse the purpose of this bill. Its passage will allow the expansion of credit unions. In the area where I live these unions are a force for development. They are fulfilling a role not served by other institutions. Their growth has been tremendous, almost fantastic.
I recall that a number of years ago a Saskatchewan Wheat Pool delegate came to a farm meeting in my area to persuade us to start a credit union. He succeeded in interesting a number of individuals who took out a few shares. A few years ago the activities of that credit union passed the $1 million mark. It is an excellent example of people in action doing for themselves the things they want to do and providing good service for themselves.
In many towns credit unions provide the only available banking services. Some years ago many branches of private banks were closed down for the sake of economy. Credit unions have stepped in to fill the gap. They
February 24, 1969

allow people to have some control over their own finances. They return excess earnings to their shareholders and in effect let their customers have money at cost.
The provisions of this bill will give the credit unions access to more funds. Passage of this bill will help the whole co-operative movement which is of great assistance to the farm community and to many urban sectors. This movement serves as a good balance wheel in our economy. I am pleased that the government has seen fit to introduce this bill and I hope it will have the approval of the house.

Mr. Speaker, credit unions in small communities are much more effective than many other types of financial houses. X understand one of the purposes of this bill is to provide for the transfer of surplus funds from one area to another, which I favour.
There is a housing factory in my area. The bill sponsored by the hon. member for Gren-ville-Carleton (Mr. Blair) regarding another financial institution, which was discussed in the house a few days ago, would make money available for loans to larger cities and towns. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford), will be joining us here in just a moment or two. He did not expect this measure to be called so soon, but he is now on his way to the chamber. subtopic: PROHIBITION OF ADVERTISING, SALE AND IMPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one can only welcome this bill

to prohibit the marketing of hazardous products and can only wonder why it took the government so long to get around to it. With particular reference to the hazardous ingredients in model plane glue, if this bill had been passed a year ago lives might well have been saved. It is not my intention to review the tragic roster of young children and some adults who have been found dead as a result of uninformed glue-sniffing, in many cases not even aware of the lethal effects. My only hope now is that the government will move with determination and force to keep these dangerous substances out of the hands of children and will not allow the prohibitory effect of the bill to be nullified by permissiveness in the regulations.
The minister and the officers of his department know as well as I do that the toxic substance in model plane glue is deadly dangerous, that young children have been induced by their friends to dabble in dangerous experimentation and that some have died. Therefore I wonder why the minister has placed this substance in a category in Part II of the schedule where the door can be opened to permissiveness under the regulations. If this happens and if definite action is not taken in spite of all the pressure that may be brought-and we know there is pressure-I warn the minister he will not have the confidence of the Canadian people. No one can tell me it is not possible for chemical companies who are always boasting about their research staffs to find a substitute for the toxic product in airplane glue or other model glues. It is up to them. It is not up to us to do their work for them.
I should like to bring to the attention of the house an article which appeared in the Toronto Star for January 25, 1969, which says in part:
The development of new, harmless glues in the U.S. should soon make it possible to ban the toxic varieties altogether. One of these was developed at the request of New York schools and it has turned out to be an effective, all-purpose glue.
It is not up to this house, nor is it up to Canadian parents to encourage or tolerate a dilatory attitude on the part of the authorities. I say to the minister "Get this stuff off the market, and the sooner the better". Let the companies find a substitute that will not endanger the lives and health of children. This should have been done many months ago. It is an extremely urgent situation. That is why it is hard to understand the apparent lethargy with which the government has proceeded with this legislation. There is certainly
February 24, 1969

Hazardous Substances
no problem about getting it through this chamber. Every member is in favour of it and most people have been clamouring for it. That is why it should have been brought in earlier.
But now that we have it before us I am rather surprised at the inclusion in part II of the schedule, among substances like bleaches and other generally non-fatal substances, of this dangerous and toxic ingredient which has caused a number of deaths in Canada. Why is not airplane glue in part I so it would simply be prevented from coming into Canada? What is the thinking behind this stranger arrangement? I ask the minister that question. The minister is not here; he will have to read it in Hansard. He has his experts to advise him, but they are not here either. He should be able to obtain an answer. With that proviso- and I warn the minister it is a serious one because I am not joking about this matter- speaking for the party I represent I say we warmly support the bill. We do express the view, however, that it should have been brought in at a much earlier stage when lives could have been saved, and, second, we insist with all seriousness that there must not, regardless of pressure, be any loophole in the regulations which would permit the continued importation into Canada of this dangerous substance so that it could fall into the hands of young people.
Before this measure passes I should like to hear an assurance from the minister concerning the reason the name of the ingredient found in model plane glue has been placed in part II of the schedule with generally nontoxic substances. Second, I should like the assurance that no loophole will appear in the regulations whereby this substance can find its way into the hands of children. Once these assurances are forthcoming we will all feel better about this bill.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak very briefly in support in general terms of Bill S-26, to prohibit the advertising, sale and importation of hazardous products, I wish, on the one hand, to commend the government for bringing this measure before us and, on the other hand, to join with the previous speaker who regretted that it has taken so long to have this legislation brought forward. There is no doubt in my mind that had this legislation been brought in five or ten years ago many Canadians would have been saved a great deal of trouble. I certainly support the idea that it should be applied in respect of materials such as paints,
particularly the prohibition in respect of advertising, selling or importation. Household products which are hazardous may be defined generally as paints, cleansers and sanitizers. 1 am sure there will be general agreement in the house and the committee as well as in the country generally that what the government is seeking is necessary.

In adding my measure of support to this bill I should like to draw the minister's attention to two bills dealing with hazardous products which appear in my name. I hope that a recommendation in one of my bills will receive detailed consideration when this bill is referred to the committee. I refer to Bill C-118 which has to do with the labelling rather than the advertising of hazardous products. The bill refers specifically to detergents and it was introduced last October. The explanatory note states:
Many houehold products In the nature of detergents are used every day by housewives and many of them do constitute a danger to health if ingested or inhaled accidentally by children or even if used for the purposes they are intended for.

This matter might also be considered when Bill S-26 is being dealt with.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF ADVERTISING, SALE AND IMPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the two previous speakers, I should like to say how very pleased I am that this bill is being introduced today although, as was mentioned earlier, the government could have introduced it long before now.
Mr. Speaker, I think, that, on the one hand, it would have probably been easier, and even desirable that this bill be introduced a lot sooner but, on the other hand, I think that it was necessary to wait for developments, to protect the life of people by forbidding them to use certain products which can be found in almost every home and which are too often within the reach of children.
A few months ago it might have been difficult for the government to anticipate the danger of these products as it is rather difficult to anticipate that within a few months or a few years, other products might endanger the life of our fellow-citizens.
In my opinion, this bill introduced today fairly well covers all the dangers which can be brought about by certain substances contained in products of daily use.
I should like to ask the minister for some clarification with regard to this bill which, I hope, will deal not only with imported products but also with noxious products which could be manufactured in Canada. Besides, I hope that the bill will deal with products which can be marketed by some Canadian industries and which could be dangerous also for their users.
Mention is made in this bill of certain beans used in the manufacture of toys or ornamental pieces. I believe that we received some from Japan. I do not believe Japanese manufacturers wanted to endanger the life of Canadian people, but I feel it is up to the government to make sure that products used in the manufacturing of apparently harmless articles do not endanger people's life. I therefore believe the bill is justified and that nobody is opposed to it.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, we must also take steps to remove the danger from aircraft glue. But I wonder whether this is not a fad among our young people. We note-although it is not general-a certain getting-out of hand of our youth. As a matter of fact, it would seem as if some young people were seeking things they cannot find in well-organized environments, that is adventure. Well, they have found it in glue sniffing which permits them to get intoxicated, to get high. Buying glue is easier

than buying cigarettes, marijuana, opium or other drugs. I believe the government should take steps in order to prohibit the sale of such products or to cope with the situation, as was mentioned a while ago by an hon. member from Edmonton, by inducing manufacturers to change their manufacturing process and make a non-poisonous product.
The same could also be said about plastic bags. They have been known to cause death, and can still do so. It is often suggested that their users should destroy them as soon as possible or perforate them.
Many other household objects can affect health, and even cause death. Consider, for instance, the excessive use of alcohol. Some people lose their health because of it. To my mind, the government has done very little to date to educate the people about the dangers of alcoholism. I would not go so far as to ask the government to past a law forbidding its use, because at times, alcohol can be useful; but when it is used unwisely, it can affect health and even lead to death. Alcohol is also, indirectly, the cause of almost as many accidental deaths on our roads as can be attributed to war.
The same goes for the immoderate use of cigarettes. I do not feel that the government should be asked to forbid their use either: yet, an immoderate use of tobacco can affect one's health.
Still, these things are available to thousands of people who, very often, use them without being aware of the dangers involved.
Mr. Speaker, this bill is timely although it comes a little late for some. To my mind, its implementation will lead not only to restrictions in the imports of dangerous products, but it will also constitute a warning about their use. This measure should be accompanied by a publicity campaign so that the people might know that we do not want to restrict their freedom but that instead we wish to protect them against the dangers involved in the use of certain products.
Mr. Speaker, for those reasons, we strongly support this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the previous speakers on this subject, I am very pleased that the government is bringing in this bill and I would like to speak in favour of it. I would like, first, to make reference to two particular matters which I feel are important. One is a
February 24, 1969

subject with regard to which I brought in a private member's bill on October 15. Bill C-119 which refers to the labelling of products. The other subject is fire, which I think should also be discussed at this time. I would then like to refer to the bill itself and bring to the attention of the house an aspect which I think should be amended before the bill is passed.
On the question of safety generally, in Canada in 1966 there was a total of 11,400 fatal accidents, of which 2,200 took place in the home. A great number of these fatal accidents were caused by falls which, as we all know, are a major cause of death among the elderly. Of these fatal home accidents, 757 were caused by falls and 561 were the result of fires and explosions. There were a great number of suffocations, 327 in all. These, of course, were almost all children. There were 275 deaths from poisoning, 75 from firearms, 51 from drowning and so on.
I think it is obvious from these figures that fire and poisoning are very definite hazards in the home, and that the government should pay attention to household products. I suggest that the reason for many of these accidents is the tremendous range of household products on the market today. The consumer is faced with a bewildering array of different products from which to choose, and he or she may have no idea of their inflammability or poison content.
I think this is inevitable. As the range of choice increases, the knowledge of the properties of the products decreases correspondingly. For this reason I think it is important for the government to step into this area and assist the consumer in ascertaining what are the hazards of the products which he or she may purchase in the stores. I think that few members in this house disagree that this is a very legitimate concern of the government.
I now turn to the point which I mentioned earlier, namely fire. There are various methods whereby fabrics can be fireproofed. Unfortunately, all these methods involve considerable expense. For example, a normal household product such as a sheet can be fireproofed, but instead of costing, say, $3 as an unfireproofed product it costs $4 when fireproofed. In other words, there is an increase of 25 per cent. In addition, when fireproofed the life of the product is reduced by half. Therefore, instead of spending $3 for a sheet which will last for a certain length of time the consumer must pay the equivalent of
Hazardous Substances
$8 for the fireproofed product for the same period of time.
I think it is important to know that fireproofing is not something that simply requires regulation. It involves far more than that. In view of the fact that cotton, wool, silk, rayon and similar products are all to some degree inflammable, I think that the best the government can do is insist that manufacturers properly label their products so that, through a system of standardized labelling, the public will be able to tell at a glance the flammability of the product.
Some products should be excluded from such regulation and be banned outright because, regardless of whether the public knows of their degree of inflammability, they are a danger. In my opinion, government action should be to insist upon the proper labelling of fabrics so that the public is fully aware of the danger of fire therefrom. In this connection I might say that the public is, generally speaking, not particularly interested in fireproofing. The experience of various manufacturers selling fireproofed drapes, fibreglass drapes, is that the public is more concerned about having colourful or attractive drapes than the fireproofed product. Therefore I think the government will have to insist upon fireproof standards for all products. The public cannot be relied on to do so. I suggest that the government should insist upon proper labelling so that the public knows the danger connected with the product it is purchasing. I should now like to turn to the next problem area.
