subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CONSIDERATION OF MEASURES TO ELIMINATE INFLATION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give early consideration to measures for maintaining the purchasing power of Canadian currency by eliminating inflation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this notice of motion raises the question of the ever-increasing cost of living, the depreciation of our currency, and inflation. The cost of living aspect concerns most Canadian consumers while inflation and the depreciated value of our currency concern the economist, but essentially they are all the same thing.
In a way this is an anniversary for me because on looking back I see I first spoke on this subject in 1963, put a question on the order paper with regard to it in 1964, again spoke on it in 1966, and now in 1969 I find myself raising the question once more. There has been one important difference since I first raised it in 1963. At that time the cost of living was increasing at a rate slightly less than 2 per cent a year; now it is increasing at a rate slightly more than 4 per cent a year. My representations in 1963 and 1966, although I think eloquent, have obviously failed to achieve their purpose.
Since 1949 the cost of living in Canada has gone up slightly more than 50 per cent. That means that $1 today is worth in purchasing power slightly less than 66 cents in 1949. I compare the present time with 1949 because, as all hon. members will remember, that was
Finance
the year when we first settled down after the second world war. There was a big jump in prices after controls were removed following the termination of the war. In 1949 prices settled down and we began to have what was then termed creeping inflation at the rate of 1 or 2 per cent a year.
As I said, creeping inflation has ceased to creep and has begun to run, and we now have inflation at the rate of about 4 per cent. I realize that, as has been pointed out by many experts, the figures established by the cost of living index do not necessarily take into account improvements in quality. Part of the increased cost of goods is no doubt due in some measure to increases in quality, better and more elaborate packaging, and advertising costs. We get our quid pro quo for advertising costs through free radio and television programs and that sort of thing. Nevertheless, after taking due account of all those factors, undoubtedly the value of our money is going down and the cost of living is going up.
The point I would like to make is that inflation is basically a tax. I believe that most economists would agree with this or at any rate would agree that inflation has the same result as a tax. It is a particularly regressive type of tax because it has the same effect as a sales tax on everything that is bought. In other words, now that we are having inflation at the rate of 4 per cent a year, it is the same thing as if the federal government set a universal sales tax at that rate on everything that is bought and on every transaction of purchase and sale in the country. The inflation tax is a tax for which the federal government is basically responsible, and I think every federal government should take the responsibility for this tax. I think it should be recognized as a tax.
Now let us consider who collects the inflation tax. I think that the government collects about a third of the total cost of the inflation tax to the consumer. I say that because it is generally recognized that governments today take about a third of the gross national product. Let us say that one-third of this tax which is levied upon everyone in the country, on every purchase and sale that takes place, goes to governments and presumably is used for useful purposes, so perhaps we cannot complain too much about that one-third.
Where does the other two-thirds of the tax go? It goes to any corporation or any individual who anticipates inflation and decides to raise his prices or services more than the in-

February 24, 1969
Finance
flationary rate. In other words, if a doctor or a businessman anticipates that there is going to be inflation at the rate of 4 per cent and is at all smart, he will sit down at the beginning of the year and say to himself that there is going to be inflation in Canada at the rate of 4 per cent and that in order to stay even and to make the same amount as last year he will have to raise the price on his goods or services by at least 4 per cent; but if he can raise it by 5 per cent he will make a bit more. So it is my guess that while governments get about one-third of the proceeds of this general inflationary sales tax, two-thirds go to those people who are well organized enough, smart enough or quick enough on their economic feet to anticipate inflation and profit by it. It is well established that there are people in any country who profit substantially from inflation and two-thirds of any inflationary sales tax goes to them.
When governments get one-third and two thirds goes to unnamed individuals and corporations which make up our economy, we know who gets the tax. But who pays for it? Obviously some of the people who pay the tax are those who are stupid enough to own government bonds or any bonds; because if you own a $100 bond at the beginning of the year and there is inflation at the rate of 4 per cent, at the end of the year your bond is worth only $96 in terms of purchasing power. So anyone who is stupid enough to own a bond, a mortgage or any instrument evidencing fixed debt is hit by the tax in full measure. Also, anyone who owns insurance policies or anyone who is on a fixed pension gets hit by it. The income of retired civil servants, for instance, has remained the same but at the same time it has been cut down in value every year by the inflationary rate which, as I said, is now at 4 per cent.
I can recall when a pension of $250 a month was considered a very generous and large pension for a retired civil servant who had spent half his life in the service of the federal government. Such a pension might have been adequate ten years ago but certainly is no longer adequate because of inflation. Those are the people who own debt instruments, widows, orphans and pensioners, unorganized wage earners and salaried people. These are the people who pay the general sales tax of which I spoke.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Obviously, therefore, the people who pay the tax are in most cases the ones who are least able to afford to pay it. For this reason
[Mr. Wahn.l
it is natural that government should want to protect them in some way. Governments do try to protect these people to some extent. For example, under the Canada Pension Plan it has been agreed that the pension payments should rise as the cost of living rises. However, I believe there is a limit of 2 per cent a year placed on such an increase and, if so, it is not enough because the cost of living is rising by 4 per cent a year.
If we permit inflation to continue there must be ever-increasing government intervention to protect people against the effects of this particular tax. Increasingly massive intervention by the government in the economy will be necessary to give these people the protection they obviously need. Indeed, in the final analysis the whole process is self-defeating. If we begin compensating, through escalation provisions, for the increase in the cost of living, we increase the rate of inflation still further. It is like a dog chasing its own tail. He goes faster and faster but he cannot catch it. If he were to do so he would be very surprised.
In our case, we cannot catch up. Any suggestion that we can compensate all those segments of the population which cannot protect themselves, by writing in escalation provisions, is unsound. This would not provide effective protection. Many times in this house suggestions have been made that the government should, for example, increase the pensions of retired civil servants. This question comes up regularly and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) just as regularly points out that the matter is being constantly considered. I believe these pensions should be increased because in my view we have a special responsibility toward retired civil servants. But if these pensions are increased, what about all those people who retired under private pension plans? They contributed to the economy too. They have no claim upon their employers for larger pensions. If the retired civil servants get a pension increase should not the holders of private pensions be treated in the same way? So one could go on from one group to another, never finding it possible to achieve equity in these circumstances.
Very often one meets people who say that inflation is not nearly as bad as it is made out to be because, though the cost of living has certainly risen, disposable income in the hands of consumers has risen even more. Of course it has, because productivity has been constantly increasing and, obviously, if
February 24, 1969

productivity goes up and if there is inflation, total disposable income must increase. But the question is: who got this increase? This argument really involves the hardship of averages. Total disposable income has increased faster than inflation because of increased productivity. The averages conceal the fact that many people who are least able to protect themselves have suffered a very large reduction in their effective purchasing power, though others who are better able to protect themselves have received substantial increases. In other words, the rich get richer and the poor get poorer whenever the state permits continuing inflation.
Someone on the other side said all this was the responsibility of the federal government which fortunately, at the present time, happens to be a Liberal government. I agree it is the responsibility of the federal government. There is even a provision in the Criminal Code which deals with the clipping of our coinage; it used to be section 398, and I have referred to it in this chamber on previous occasions. It says:
Everyone who impairs, diminishes or lightens a current gold or silver coin with intent that it should pass for a current gold or silver coin... is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for 14 years.
So this is a serious offence. Yet recently there was a wholesale exchange of our silver currency and nickel was substituted for silver. In other words, our currency was lightened very substantially so far as silver content is concerned, in the course of quite a normal transaction. It thus appears that one can practice coin lightening provided it is done on a large enough scale, when it ceases to be a criminal offence and becomes a legitimate operation of high finance.
To show that this is not just a concern of mine but that it is fairly general, I should like to refer to something which was said by Professor Clark in his report on social security submitted to this house some years ago. He was asked who suffered most from inflation and the rising cost of living, and he replied as follows:
Inflation is inherently unfair to those economically or politically incapable of defending their interests. This includes some categories of salaried employees and those on pension-both private and government. Recipients of government old age pensions are in a position to exert some political pressure on their own behalf-
As we have seen.
-but those on private pension usually have little opportunity, and no contractual claim to have their pensions raised to offset inflation since their
Finance
retirement. Those widows, orphaned children and retired persons who are largely dependent financially on the proceeds of life insurance policies, annuities, interest on government or corporate bonds, or other investments at fixed, or nearly fixed, rates of interest, suffer from inflation with no prospect of relief.
Professor Kenneth Boulding, using somewhat less academic language, puts it this way:
Inflation is a refined method of taking bread out of the mouths of the aged, the infirm, the widows and orphans.
Some views on this subject have also been expressed in recent years by the Economic Council of Canada and also by Mr. Ras-minsky, the respected Governor of the Bank of Canada. At one time there were people who said a little inflation was good for the economy, that if there was not inflation at the rate of 1.5 per cent or 2 per cent a year there would be high unemployment rates, and that to keep the economy prospering a little creeping inflation was necessary. More recently it has been recognized that any degree of inflation is bad for us. Since this is an important point, I should like to quote a statement made by Mr. Grajiam Towers in January of this year. Mr. Towers was at one time Governor of the Bank of Canada. He was referring to a suggestion that a little creeping inflation was good for the economy.
In discussing the thesis that we can and should accept inflation as a means of achieving high rates of output, the Governor of the Bank of Canada in his last annual report expressed the opinion that this option is not really open to us. He said, and I quote "It would soon become just as difficult to prevent price rises from exceeding a high target rate as it now is to prevent them from exceeding a low target rate. The same policies of restraint would come to be required. Nothing would be gained in employment or output; the difficult efforts to adjust to inflation would thus have been to no avail and our ability to grow steadily would be continuously threatened by the impairment of our international competitive position."
A little later Mr. Towers said:
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Another evil of accepting a certain degree of inflation as inevitable and tolerable is that it tends to make governments complacent. Why take politically unpopular measures to fight a rise in the general price level if a little inflation is part of the so-called "trade-off" against unemployment? Eventually, of course, steps have to be taken if only because substantially rising living costs are widely unpopular. But by that time the problem is more difficult to solve and all kinds of disruptions and distortions have occurred. Moreover, one can never in this modern world get back to the level of prices and the cost of living that prevailed in earlier years. So I believe that governments should and must set their faces against

February 24, 1969
Finance
any continuing rises in the general level of prices. They may not be 100 per cent successful. But, if they try hard, they should be able to do a pretty fair job and avoid the quite disastrous effects of destroying public confidence in the value of money. If, on the other hand, governments accept continuing inflation as inevitable, even to a limited degree-often defined as 1or 2 per cent per annum -they are defeated before they start.
Before concluding perhaps I might also mention the effect of inflation upon what is of concern to all of us, namely, very high interest rates. Let us consider for a moment what happens when there is a 4 per cent rate of inflation. Suppose you go to a corporation which perhaps is in the 50 per cent tax bracket, or to an individual whose top income is in a tax bracket of 50 per cent, to borrow $100. This company or individual knows that if they grant you a loan of $100, at the end of one year, with a 4 per cent rate of inflation, they will get back only $96 worth of purchasing power. Therefore they must charge you 8 per cent interest just to stay even. We must remember that they are paying an income tax of 50 per cent on the interest and they have to cope with a 4 per cent increase in inflation. By charging 8 per cent interest the loss in purchasing power by making the loan to you is just cancelled out. Therefore it is pretty apparent that the combined effect of inflation and income tax rates at that level are bound to make interest costs high. There is really no way to keep them low except by subsidization. The problem we are facing in raising money for housing mortgages and other useful purposes at the present time is largely due to this factor I have mentioned-inflation.

speechtext: Order, please. I regret I have to inform the hon. member that his time has expired.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CONSIDERATION OF MEASURES TO ELIMINATE INFLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I heartily concur in this motion because in its terms it is as good a motion of non-confidence in this government as one could possibly devise. The hon. member says that he has put forward this motion in these terms since about 1963. That could be. But in discussing this subject I find myself in the position of not wanting to repeat my budget speech and other speeches made this year about finance.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CONSIDERATION OF MEASURES TO ELIMINATE INFLATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CONSIDERATION OF MEASURES TO ELIMINATE INFLATION
speechtext:
The poor Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) might perhaps suddenly decide there was some truth in what he said about inflation, having
[Mr. Wahn.l
been a member of the administration in the past that blithely disregarded inflation and told us that it was nothing very serious. However, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has belatedly decided to lay the cornerstone of some sort of policy. Having seen the problem he now says he is taking care of it. He said that on television during the course of the winter, I think around New Year, and has gone around preaching restraint on the part of others but not the government.
I agree entirely with what the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn) said about the reaction of the public to the spending policies of the federal government. The minister has been raising spending limits for this coming year to the tune of $900 million. We have had a budgetary deficit that was acknowledged in the estimates at the time to be some $730 million. We have also had some supplementary estimates in the amount of some $151 million, though the figures do not quite jibe in view of what the expenditures are now and what they were said to be at the time of the budget. I would say that the net result is roughly another $100 million expenditure. These supplementary estimates are Supplementary Estimates B. I am waiting to see the final estimates which will include the bill for agricultural price supports and a number of other matters. These will come in around the end of March.
I do not agree with my hon. friend from St. Paul's when he says that inflation is entirely the responsibility of the federal government. The federal government must provide leadership in meeting inflation but inflation, regardless of the way you measure it, results from the increase in wages, the difference between the demand for a return and the increase in the production of goods and services. That is what it comes down to and it is a modem phenomenon.
On the other hand I think the federal government can slough off some responsibility on to some of the provincial administrations. Most of the provincial premiers will declare that they have had a 15-year honeymoon, that they have gone on spending and spending until they have come to the horrible realization at the present time that they have to cut back their spending. This year we will see some agonizing reappraisals of provincial policies, but we will see some much greater agonizing reappraisals on the part of the federal government. One of these reappraisals will concern medicare. If there ever is a penny-wise, pound-foolish program it is medicare
February 24, 1969

as presently designed. The Minister of Finance has to be credible in his government policies. One has only to note our bond prices to realize that the market does not for a moment believe the government.
The hon. member for St. Paul's gave us quite an academic dissertation on the causes and effects of inflation. Certainly the bond market is hedging against the inflation. Incidentally, in recent weeks we have observed that the cost of living index has changed its base, 1961 now equalling 100. I looked at the returns that came into my office this morning. They were most interesting. Today the cost of living index has risen to 122; under the former 1949 index, which I agree was a little unrealistic, we would be up to 160. If anyone is interested in this, the cost of living for the average individual last month rose by .27 per cent. The index is already almost four points higher than it was in January, 1968.
This sort of thing cannot continue. The government must show leadership by cutting expenditure, not by adding $900 million to budgeted expenditures. The Minister of Finance says it will be only $900 million, but quite frankly I do not believe him. I think it will be more than that. He has made no changes in his post-secondary educational program, nor in the hospital insurance program. He now wants to start on medicare. The first two programs have been blamed for the increase in costs. Lessons have been learned and the appropriate steps should be taken.
I would have thought that the recent speeches made by the Governor of the Bank of Canada were an absolute "back of the hand" from Canada's central banker to his superiors, the government, an indication that their spending policies were entirely unreasonable and unrealistic in view of the problems existing today. The provinces must share some responsibility. The drive or impetus is there whether it is municipal, provincial or federal. Currencies of other countries have been debased as a result of inflation. It makes no difference whether this inflation is slow, creeping or galloping. On the one hand the people are encouraged to be responsible, save their money and invest. On the other hand, the government is asking for permission to nibble away at these savings by establishing the Canada Development Corporation.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
As there are many others who wish to speak, I will limit myself to those remarks. I
Finance
am glad to have had the opportunity to speak on this motion. I commend it to all hon. members on the government side. May it
pass.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CONSIDERATION OF MEASURES TO ELIMINATE INFLATION
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CONSIDERATION OF MEASURES TO ELIMINATE INFLATION
speechtext:
Not right now; do you mind if I complete my remarks?
This government shares all the broad goals which every civilized government in the

February 24, 1989
Finance
world shares, such as full employment, economic growth, price stability, balance in external trade. Unlike the opposition, the government has to reconcile all the diametrically opposed elements within this objective which occur on a day to day basis. This is not easy to do. The government is fully aware of the fact that as long as there is inflation people will get hurt, mainly the older people and the poor. Elderly people who have given service have every right to believe they should be able to live without undue stress and strain in their old age. Nobody wants inflation. On the business side, inflation leads to troubles with which we are all familiar.
It is difficult to obtain money to invest in an enterprise. It is particularly difficult to get mortgage and bond money, which is the type of money required for government and social long term objectives. It has been suggested if people would restrain their wage demands, we would no longer have inflation. It is true higher wages help cause inflationary problems. Management helps cause inflationary problems when it is less than careful with expense accounts, or less than diligent in having the most up to date equipment in factories to cut down production costs. Management not only hurts operational efficiency and the workers' ability to produce, but society as a whole, when through selfish motives production machinery is allowed to become run down.
There are two sides to this question. There are those who want high tariffs for inefficient industries to hide behind. The problem is a broad one which has to be attacked in many ways. As the hon. member for Edmonton West intimated, it is not something for which we can completely blame the worker. A great deal of the inflation is caused by government spending. This government should not be criticized for attempting to rationalize spending and bring it under control. Instead of saying to the provinces you can have 50 per cent of X dollars, the federal government is attempting to define X dollars and the objectives for which those dollars will be used in order to rationalize and control its budget. I have great confidence that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) will be able to bring his budget under control. It will take time because rationalization will have to result from discussions with provincial governments. Provincial governments must use restraint, as must the federal government.
The new department of regional development is a great step toward rational growth

in areas where it is desperately needed without fanning the flames of inflation. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) has proposed the creation of an independent public agency to study, investigate and report on the problems of rising costs and prices. There is no one single solution. I am confident that this government has as good brains as any government ever had. which is all one can hope to find. This government is attempting to solve a situation which has not been solved conclusively by any government anywhere. I would be less than honest if I did not say the government must be like Caesar's wife; it must appear to be irreproachable as well as being irreproachable.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
A greater effort must be made by the government to spend less money frivolously on offices, to restrain itself. The government should think twice about expenditures that the public will take as examples of frivolous spending because people will say, "What the hell; if they are doing it, I will do it too."
There are areas in which we can all help the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). I would suggest that we, ourselves, think twice about whether we want an office repainted. Nobody has asked, me, as a backbencher, if I want mine repainted. If they did, I would probably try to act like a good Canadian and fight inflation by saying, "Let it be for a while." There are attitudes that members of the government can take that will help the general climate, that will help the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance to achieve their objectives. These objectives, to a great extent can be achieved by themselves, but to an equally great extent they have to be achieved by example.
I would like to close by reading from the economic report of the President of the United States to congress in January, 1969, which included the annual report of the council of economic advisers in the United States with respect to combating inflation:
It requires clear comprehension by all groups of the overwhelming importance of this goal.
We are doing good things. We should continue to try to do those things and more. We should continue to try to set a good example in our own house so that people will not say, "If the government can spend money like this, then I can do it too."

Order, please. I hope hon. members will not mind if I bring to their
February 24, 1969

attention the fact that a number of hon. members are anxious to participate in this debate and we are running short of time.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CONSIDERATION OF MEASURES TO ELIMINATE INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this is the kind of debate in which so many members wish to participate, I shall restrict myself to fewer remarks than I might have made otherwise. I have found that few worthwhile suggestions about inflation have been made in the debate to this point. Everyone is against inflation. We all realize that inflation creates problems. I am not at all sure that the previous speaker's suggestion that he would not repaint his office would make any significant contribution to the struggle against inflation in the Canadian economy. However, it was a worthy gesture on his part.
We must really ask the question, and it is a question which has not yet been asked, why have we got inflation? In my opinion, the answer is that we have reached a position where those who are strong in the market place laugh at the market place. Adam Smith may be dead a couple of hundred years but it is only today that his theory is being buried. Those able to dominate the market place and fix prices in oligopolistic industries are not subject to the kind of forces discussed in the day of Adam Smith. This is what we have to recognize. When the strong ignore the dictates of the market place, when competition has ceased to be a significant factor in our life, or as significant as it used to be, then the weak are going to suffer.
The answers are not easy; they are not simple. I, for one, face the future with some hesitation because I think the result is inevitable. Unless we bring in some measure of price control, we are not going to solve the problem of inflation. We are now getting the worst of both worlds. We are getting inflation and high unemployment. At one time one would have thought that if we had the kind of unemployment we have at present in Canada, inflation would have been contained. But that obviously is not the case now. Unemployment is not working to offset inflation. Unless we bring in some measure of price control, or at least a prices review board, we cannot stop inflation.
The question of adjustment in pensions was raised. This must be government policy because no matter what measures we may take to contain inflation, inevitably there will be some industries that must have their prices raised. Industries in which productivity
Finance
cannot increase as quickly as in others will want to raise their prices and competition will have to be made to work in such cases. We shall have to make some very significant changes in our tax system.
I would like to deal for a moment with advertising and selling costs. We have a situation where it is obvious that the economy is under some strain so far as price increases are concerned. But what is happening? Everybody is breaking his neck to try and get people to borrow more money to buy things that are not really necessary. One of the difficulties is that advertising almost nullifies the government's attempts to encourage restraint. It is like trying to hold back the flood waters, and I think the government should have taken a lesson from King Canute.
I was particularly disturbed by the phrase used by the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn) when he said it was stupid to own government bonds. Mr. Speaker, we are having enough trouble selling government bonds without supporters of the government adding to the problems of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). In some ways the government is responsible for the position in respect of bonds because the tax system as it now exists discriminates against the holders of government bonds. On the one hand we say, "Buy our bonds," and then we design a tax system which says, "Bonds are a bad thing for you to buy."
Certain things, like dividends from equity in Canadian corporations, are deductible from taxable income but income from bonds is not deductible. If we are serious about reducing the price of government financing we should neutralize the tax system, and realize that it is usually people of limited means who invest in government bonds. We should make it possible for income from government bonds to be deductible for tax purposes.
A country has only so many resources, whether in manpower or in money. It is very important that we start thinking in terms of planning our economy and the way we can allocate resources, because we must remember that what goes into one sector cannot go into another sector. We have to make some value judgments about what is important in our society and what sort of activities should receive the most resources. We have failed to do this, and it is important that we do it. Otherwise, the war on poverty and our efforts to overcome regional disparities will fall on barren ground. There is much more I would like to say on this subject but since there are

February 24, 1969
Finance
other hon. members who wish to speak I conclude by saying that I appreciate having had the opportunity of saying these few words.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CONSIDERATION OF MEASURES TO ELIMINATE INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment a number of those who have already spoken on this subject. They have dramatized for all of us the seriousness of this question of inflation, but to state the seriousness of the problem is not to solve it. I was particularly interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) since he was prepared to admit that the federal government alone is not responsible for inflation or for curing it. I think this is something we too often overlook. Too often when there is a problem, we take the attitude "Well, let the government settle it."
The hon. member who spoke after the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn) indicated that restraint was necessary, that we all had a responsibility for restraint. I think the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) underlined this when he referred to market power. Market power I believe is a significant concept in this discussion of inflation both from the point of view of those who are selling goods and those who are offering their services in the form of organized labour. Those who are in a position, because of their particular situation, to extract an 18 per cent increase in wage rates are in a position to affect unit costs. When this sort of thing occurs with some frequency, such people are in a position to affect the climate of opinion just as those who are selling goods and services and are in a position of market power can abuse their position. What I am attempting to say here is that inflation is very largely a question of attitude. It is very largely affected by one's expectations of the future. I think the federal government has recognized this problem and has underlined it on a number of occasions. I believe the budget presented to this house on October 22 underlined the government's attitude when the minister introduced measures which will balance the budget.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The minister underlined the seriousness of inflation when he met head on this whole question of expectation, the need to show those who are most concerned that we can in fact manage our economy. In this connection, I should like to say a word or two about the effects of inflation. Too often we talk about

inflation as if the taxpayers who will suffer are not also lenders. I am suggesting that the beneficiaries of social security programs, such as pensions and life insurance, are also those who are the lenders in the final analysis. Their premiums are the savings which buy the bonds that are the basis of investment in the private companies in Canada. These savings also underwrite and finance government programs. I am saying that the lender is not the large institution, is not the life insurance company, is not the pension fund, but is the person whose premiums flow into the pension fund, or into the life insurance companies and which are invested on his behalf.
I believe that too often we tend to regard inflation as something which affects only a few, the weak. So it does; frequently, they are affected more than anybody else. I am concerned about this because they are least able to defend themselves. Equally, however, inflation affects almost everyone in Canada. Almost everyone in Canada now has an interest in a pension plan. I think the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn), when he referred to inflation as a tax, was accurate. I believe it is a tax. Not only does it tax everyone, but it taxes those least able to defend themselves. But inflation is not something which is generated only within a country; it is generated as well by events outside a country. I believe that in Canada we are particularly sensitive to the actions of the United States in this regard. Over 70 per cent of our trade is with the United States. What happens in the United States affects us quickly. The United States has been concerned with a major inflationary problem and has imposed a 10 per cent surtax on income taxes to cope with this problem.
I should like to add as well that I share the view of the hon. member for St. Paul's with regard to creeping inflation. I think the Economic Council gave more credibility than it should have to that suggestion by calling it a trade-off. I think the trade-off between a certain percentage of inflation, perhaps 1.4 per cent, to obtain the 3 per cent employment rate which the economic council says is a goal is no more than an invitation to the very thing to which the hon. member was referring. I was happy to see that the Governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Rasminsky, in a recent speech abroad drew attention to this question. He said:
Expressions of concern about inflation sometimes draw the reply that we must choose between inflation and unacceptable rates of unemployment. I think we are today seeing more and more evidence that this is an illusion.
February 24, 1969

I should also like to draw the attention of the house to the fact that government policies are starting to bear fruit in this area. In the issue of the Globe and Mail for February 21 under the heading "Problem sector showing gains" there is an article which contains the following information:
During the past four months the rate of unemployment has dropped steadily from 5.1 per cent of the labour force in October to 4.3 per cent in January, after adjustment for seasonal factors. The rise in the consumer price index, on a year-to-year basis, declined during the same period from 4.2 per cent to 3.8 per cent.

subsubtopic: PROHIBITION OF ADVERTISING, SALE AND IMPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the adjournment at six o'clock I was discussing hazardous products, in particular the inflammability of garments. Let me point out briefly that this is not the only problem which this bill is meant to cover. There are a great many other aspects to it, poisoning notably among them. In view of the fact we are perhaps a little short of time I will leave it to other members to discuss these other aspects, and move on to the Bill itself.
Hazardous Substances
The actual wording of Bill S-26 in its present form is not acceptable to me, and it is my hope that at the committee stage and on third reading other members will consider seriously the points I will be bringing forward this evening. I am not a member of the committee and thus I ask for your indulgence in allowing me to mention at this time the specific provisions of this bill to which I take exception.
Clause 8, subclause (3) would require that any amendment made by the Governor In Council to the schedule of this bill must be placed before this house within two years of it being brought forward as an order in council. My personal view is that this would result in this bill being amended every year, for no minister could risk leaving these amendments to the final year. Keeping in mind the amount of legislation the government house leader wishes us to consider this year, would place an intolerable burden on this house and result in a serious uncertainty in the law. For example, as a result of an election or delay in passing legislation we may well be unable to deal with this specific amending legislation, and the various hazardous substances which the Governor In Council had decided should not be placed on the market would once more become available for sale in Canada. This is what I mean by uncertain law.
If you look at subsection 3 of section 8 sir, you will see that the Governor In Council is prohibited from bringing back any of these particular items which had been dropped from the list as a result of not being brought before Parliament. This would mean considerable uncertainty which would, I regret to say, result in hazardous products being placed on the market from time to time with attendant danger to the consumers, particularly children.
The essence of this legislation in my mind should be to allow the minister or the Governor In Council to act with speed. We do not want to have a dangerous toy sold in Canada for a period of time before something can be done about it, nor do we want this toy to come back on the market through too rigid legislation. We want to have something done quickly. A subsection such as subsection (3) of section 8 would nullify the intent of this legislation.
Let me give notice that if this measure goes to the committee and I am unable to have my views adopted there, I will propose an amendment to this house at the third reading

February 24, 1969
Hazardous Substances
stage. I will suggest that, instead of having a period of only two years during which time such orders in council can be presented to this house, we should have a period of perhaps eight years. This should meet the objections to the original bill of those who put in section 8(3). The bill should certainly not be amended by parliament every two years, but should remain in force for a substantially longer interval, namely eight years. Perhaps eight years is too short a period of time, and it should be longer but eight years is my suggestion.
If this bill is passed in its present form it would introduce an element of uncertainly and risk into the law. This is always unfortunate. If the legislation is examined, it will be seen that section 9 allows for a board of review, which is flexible and allows sufficient or adequate appeal from decisions of the Governor in Council. If we carry on with section 8(3) as it now is we would be introducing a guarantee which in my opinion is quite unnecessary and indeed damaging to the object of the bill. With those remarks, I will resume my seat. While I support the bill, I sincerely hope the committee will take note of my remarks. If it does not and the bill comes back to the house in its present form, I will propose an amendment along the lines I have suggested.

I expect wise and solemn decisions from this side of the house, but in the light of experience during this session I am somewhat doubtful of the decisions which come from the government side. The government, through the medium of the minister and his officials and after what I presume was long and careful consideration, has carefully enumerated specific products which in part I are the subject of outright prohibition within the terms of the bill and in part II are the subject of conditional prohibition.
This is the basis on which I put it. If what the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich said is correct, and that is what the minister and his officials had in mind when they first
February 24, 1969

framed the terms of this legislation, why-have a schedule at all? Why did they not simply give to the Governor in Council the right to say that any product which had been examined had been deemed to be hazardous in accordance with the provisions of this act? We have a schedule because the government and its officials, having examined the whole range of products, have said this specific product and that named product are to be brought under the schedule. I accept this. As one who has lived in a household with children for many years, this defect in our law has long been apparent.
I believe that other approaches could have been made to meet the evil that exists, and provisions could have been framed in other ways. There is an evil in this respect. There has been a gap in our law, and I am glad to see that the government is attempting to deal with it. However, it is completely wrong to suggest that, because this is the case, we should give to the Governor in Council the right to add new products, without any limiting conditions.
I have said in this house on many occasions that it is necessary in the age in which we live to give to the government the right to move swiftly, firmly and directly if a product is put on the market, a toy or anything else, that is hazardous. If a government, when operating under this legislation, is of the opinion that a product should not be allowed on the market because of its dangerous characteristics, the government should have the right to move and should not have to wait until parliament meets in order to secure amendments to the legislation.
There should be the right to move swiftly and decisively in this regard. But if the government decided it was essential to secure the consent and approval of the majority of the members of this house and of the other place to say that certain products were hazardous, why should it not have to come here after taking care of the immediate danger to ask that additional products be added to the list?
I can see no danger arising when the government moves by order in council under the provisions of clause 8 of the bill. Then, the product cannot be sold because it falls squarely within the terms of the bill. There is a board of review in this respect. If the manufacturers, producers, or anyone affected wishes to do so, they can ask the minister to establish a board of review and in this way might be able to overcome the impediment which the bill places upon them. But if this is 29180-373
Hazardous Substances
not the case and parliament has not said that product A, B or C is in fact a hazardous product, the government is compelled within the period of two years to come back to parliament to secure the approval of this house and the other place before the views of the government can be sustained.
This is apparent from a reading of the transcript of the proceedings in the other place and the statements made in the committee. I suggest that the attempt by the government to circumvent this very wise and sensible decision by persuading its members to secure amendments to comply with the government line is wrong. I hope there are members on the other side of the house who hear or will read what I have to say and will consult with the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) about this.

I suggest to them that in the light of the question of privilege which was raised, and which Your Honour held was not a question of privilege but which aroused some controversy, they will show the people of Canada that they will not toe the government line.
I will be happy to rise in my place when this bill comes back here if government members have in fact, as I hope they will, in co-operation with members of the opposition stood squarely against the government and the minister in their attempt to remove this amendment from the bill. I hope they will stand against that attempt and return the bill to this house unimpaired and with this amendment still in it.
I have been trying to be objective in these remarks. I have tried to rise above politics. I will try to rise even further now. This bill is a clear illustration of one of the grave defects in our political and constitutional system. The only way the minister can deal with this problem is to invoke the criminal law, as is the case with so many of the other aspects of

February 24, 1969

our social structure which come under his jurisdiction, such as restrictive trade practices.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
When the government tabled in the house its position paper for the federal-provincial conference with regard to constitutional change, there was one aspect of it which appealed to me very greatly, namely the proposition that the highest courts of the land will not be bound by the principle of stare dicisis. In other words, with regard to constitutional law-and this has been a great defect for many years-the highest court in our country is free, if it so chooses, on the facts which are brought before it, to disregard previous judicial decisions of either the Privy Council or the Supreme Court of Canada and to come to different conclusions. I am not suggesting that the Court should legislate to the extent which at times the Supreme Court of the United States does, but I do think there is room for a greater degree of freedom and for far more flexibility. I hope that the provinces will accept this proposal.
In any event, I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) and the government will seek ways and means of trying to bring about a change in our judicial practice at the highest level so that the Supreme Court will be entitled to disregard previous decisions. This is an example of a case where the government should not be compelled to try to circumvent the constitution, as judicially interpreted, by invoking the criminal law. The problem should be dealt with by regulation, the breach of which shall be punished by suitable penalties. The government should have the right to regulate and control, a right which does not exist at the present time.
I would like to think that, just as important as some of the other problems to which the Prime Minister has referred and which have been placed on the agenda of federal-provincial conferences, would be issues which affect so many millions of people, as certainly this bill does. Surely, the provinces brought together at the common table to discuss these matters with the federal government would be prepared to say that in many areas of our social, political and cultural life there is a means of giving the federal government the power to act and to regulate. I stand four square for the preservation of provincial authority in many aspects of our life. It is essential to keep those aspects on the basis on

which they were established in the constitution on which our confederation was established. But in view of the mobility of people today we should be entitled to expect a uniformity of regulations and legislation in matters of this kind.
So, I say to the minister in all sincerity that I hope he and his colleagues will use their influence with the Prime Minister and with the Minister of Justice to see that matters of this kind are brought to the stage where we no longer have to worry about being able to legislate. When we come to deal with some of the great problems which will affect our society, problems such as water and air pollution, we will face precisely the same difficulty long before we may have accomplished our mission of dealing with such matters as language rights. I am not one to say they are not important, but to me these subjects are equally important and in some ways more important because they affect intimately the personal lives, the comfort and safety of so many millions of people. I hope, therefore, that this aspect of Constitutional problems will be regarded as the number one priority of this government and that, irrespective of other constitutional changes, ways and means will be found to ensure the right of the federal government, possibly in cooperation with provincial governments, to proceed not by invoking the criminal law but by means of regulations.

Before commencing some of my general remarks on the bill, I would like to participate in the discussion of the specific question of the powers that the minister may have by order in council to act without coming to parliament. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) has pointed out, quite eloquently I think, the need for the minister to have authority on which to act rapidly in cases where substances come onto the market, and their chemical derivations cannot be anticipated because of the rapid changes which are taking place in technology. I believe that the minister needs some discretion to be able to take a product off the market. On the other hand, I recognize the validity of the argument put forward by the hon. member for Peace River that one cannot assign unlimited power to governments by order in council. I would like to suggest to the minister for his consideration, and this is just a thought that occurred to me as the debate was taking place, that there is another approach which we might take to this problem. We might give
February 24, 1969

to the minister the power he requires but ensure that the decision of the minister comes back to parliament. Instead of giving him unlimited power to legislate, let us give him perhaps six months. If he decides to take a product off the market, then within the six months he would come to parliament and ask parliament to put it on one of the schedules. I hope the minister, and perhaps the hon. member for Peace River, will consider this proposition as an attempt to recognize the difficulty which the minister might encounter by not having the power to remove an item from the market which is not in the schedule now but which may obviously be a hazard to health in his judgment.
I am very pleased to see this bill come before parliament. It represents one more nail in the coffin of Mr. Caveat Emptor. Mr. Buy-er-Beware has been buried with very little mourning. The government is accepting its responsibility to take a look at the hazardous substances that come on the market and to protect the public from the sale of them.
I would like to make a number of points on this subject. When the hon. member for Bran-don-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) spoke he raised the question of cigarettes as a hazardous substance. I notice that the bill does not deal with cigarettes, but where it deals with advertising it seems to give a rather broad definition of that term. I wonder whether it could not be made quite evident that it is not only advertising that will be prohibited if the substance is considered dangerous to the public. For example, if one considers cigarette advertising, the manufacturers may be anticipating that some legislation will be passed soon restricting their ability to advertise cigarettes. They are already moving into a whole new range of gimmicks which may not be classified as advertising but which may very well be transferring expenditure in the publicity department from one form of promotion to another. I refer to such things as giving-away large sums of money, cars and so on. I think that the definition of advertising should be made clearer in order to ensure that it covers all types of promotion. In some cases, such promotions may be more damaging than advertising. I am thinking of door to door sampling and things of this type. I think it is fairly important for the minister to make sure that sucji a possibility does not exist.
[DOT] (8:30 p.ra.)
There is one omission from this bill. Looking at clause 8, this bill lists what shall not be
Hazardous Substances
put on the market. I think that to be completely effective or to be more effective the bill should also include what must be put on the market. I am thinking particularly of containers which may be hazardous in themselves. They may contain hazardous or semihazardous substances, yet the container may be more dangerous than its contents-pill boxes of various kinds. I am wondering what provision the minister is considering to take care of this particular problem.
A while ago I raised the question of glue sniffing. I am pleased to see that glues are covered by this bill and that the minister will have power to remove them from sale. No one at this point can be certain what the answer to this problem might be. Eliminating the sale of glue might help in some cases, or legislation in terms of assisting persons who sniff glue by recognizing this as a psychiatric problem. I have a private members' bill to that effect.
The power to help is contained in this bill. I think all those concerned with this problem will breathe somewhat more easily knowing that, upon examination or following research, the government does have the power to take glue or substances similar to glue off the market or ask that they be modified in some way to make them less dangerous.
The overall impression I get of this bill is that while there is a schedule of some specific things such as bleaches, this term encompasses a whole area of production; namely, cleansers, sanitizers or household goods containing chlorine. There is a remarkably wide range of products covered by that definition. The impression one gets is that the minister will possess very great powers to act. Perhaps the big question which arises in my mind at this point is to what extent he will be willing to act and to what extent will he and his department be vigilant in the pursuit of these hazardous substances. It is not enough to have a bill which says certain things can be done. We know the government has all kinds of legislation now under which it could act in other areas and it has been very reluctant to take action; it has not used its power enough, rather than over-used its power, as is the fear of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin).
Let me in closing congratulate the minister on this bill. I think it is a very good step in the right direction. I indicate I will support an amendment reviving the one deleted by the Senate, perhaps putting a time factor into

I am
pleased to rise to support the legislation now before the house. I have spent the day in this chamber listening to the debates. I am impressed by the broad support which the legislation has received from all parties. Of course, this bill has very broad support in the country; it has received the attention which it deserves and requires. It provides machinery which hopefully will be used to protect the interests of consumers in a very broad way. The interests of consumers are catered to by the bill satisfactorily, in my view. There has been discussion, as well, as to the interests of parliament. Will there be a right of review later? The Senate revision remains. There has been an interesting discussion about it. I intend to support in this respect the suggestion made, notwithstanding the views of the house leader of the opposition. I would prefer to see the legislation stand, without the necessity of the house going through the awkward business of reviewing a two-year accumulation of regulations.
I should like to turn to the area of the producer because there has been no discussion today of the interests of the producer, and with respect I should like to make one suggestion for an amendment which I hope may be introduced before the bill is finally enacted, that is, an amendment to section 9. As background, may I say that a very fair right of appeal is provided for any producer who is a victim of, if I may put it that way, an order preventing the goods he has purchased or imported from being sold. Provision for appeal is made and those who have imported goods and find they are the subject of an order in council which prevents them from being sold can, under clause 9, within 60 days, ask that a board of review be constituted to consider the order in council which was passed. Unfortunately, in the normal course of events the products to be considered would be products already in existence. More than likely they would be products someone had already paid for-either the producer or the importer. The producer or the importer would have a legal right to appeal but in fact they may not have a real appeal because of the fact that there is no requirement at all in clause 9 that the appeal be dealt with within any given period.
The board might be set up in the normal course. It might review the evidence in the
IMr. Saltsman.]
normal course. However, the Board might take too long in arriving at a decision for an ordinary producer or a small producer to be able to take advantage of the right of appeal. He might find he was bankrupt with an inventory of goods which were considered hazardous and not have the opportunity, because of the fact that an appeal might not be heard in time, to save himself from what might be an injustice. In any event, I would point out that it would be most desirable to include a requirement in clause 9 that the board render a decision on the appeal within a time which would be meaningful to an ordinary producer or importer. In this connection, I suggest that a period of seven days might not be inappropriate.
Seven days is not a great deal of time within which to prepare a case, but one would hope that if an order in council had been passed against a particular product it would be supported by an investigation of the goods in question and that certain experts would be genuinely of the opinion that the goods were hazardous. So the case for the Crown, if I may put it may, would be immediately available.
If the importer or producer wished to have his case heard quickly he ought to be entitled to have it heard quickly by the representatives of the government. With that amendment, I intend to support the bill. I will support it anyway, but I do hope consideration will be given to the possibility of an injustice being suffered because an appeal is not heard in time save a producer from an unfortunate situation.

But
the original draft of this bill received more public approval than is going to be the case if this new clause 3, which the other place insisted on inserting, is passed. I say that in the interests of the consumers of this country.
Having said that, the bill is an improvement over the bill of last year. It is much
February 24, 1969

broader than the bill that was proposed last year. Instead of hazardous substances, the bill refers to the hazardous products, a broader category. In addition to chemicals, glues, household cleansers, bleaches and polishes, the bill will include articles like matches, flammable textiles, mechanical toys, electrical appliances and dangerous lawnmowers.
Under the original draft of the bill, the minister was empowered to act swiftly and decisively to ban hazardous substances directly they came on to the market and before damage was done. I agree with what my colleague said a little while ago that there is much more chance of the minister's powers being underused than overused. Although the minister and I may differ on a lot of things, I trust the Minister with powers to act quickly in putting substances that really are dangerous on the schedule and safely out of the reach of people, rather than making him come back to parliament every time he wishes to add a substance to the schedule. People are worried about parliament today because they feel parliament moves far too slowly to meet the needs of this day and age. If the minister has to come back to parliament to debate and pass a measure of this kind every time he wants to deal with a fresh hazardous product then, I think the consumers of Canada will have a perfectly legitimate grievance.
When the original bill was drafted, the Consumers Association of Canada wrote to members of parliament indicating that the bill was a good measure and they hoped it would be supported. As I say, the minister was empowered under the original bill to add any substance he thought hazardous to the schedule. I believe the minister is quite capable of using his discretion in this regard. There are many experts to assist him in his department. With all the red tape in government departments there is far more danger of the minister not using this power than overusing it.
A similar situation arose when the drug bill was in committee. Some members worried unduly about the need for the insertion of what were almost impossible safety standards. This was really an expression of lack of confidence in the food and drug directorate. I feel that until such time as the food and drug directorate errs sufficiently to lose our confidence, it merits trust. In the same way, I think that this minister and his department can be trusted sufficiently to test a substance to determine whether it is hazardous. If it is,
Hazardous Substances
it can be placed on the schedule and removed from the reach of consumers before it can do any damage and before somebody gets killed.
I should just like to refer to the proceedings in the other place when this bill came up for debate. Dr. Crawford, the Deputy Minister of National Health and Welfare was quoted. He appeared in 1967 before the Senate committee on banking and commerce and was asked how his department had dealt with the emergencies that had resulted from the appearance on the market of necklaces made from the poisonous jequirity beans and the plastic ice balls from Hong Kong which contained contaminated water. In his reply to that question Dr. Crawford stated:
Well, we had to deal with the provincial departments on this. We telephoned and telegraphed and told them of the hazard which was in their shops and they dealt with it provincially. This is how we had to handle that situation. Of course it was a pretty time consuming process.
Of course it was. If the federal government is going to show leadership in the matter of one standard of safety for necessary products for Canadians from Victoria to St. John's, the department must have some jurisdiction for determining what are hazardous substances so that they may be put on the schedule to this bill.
According to the latest available statistics in regard to accidents in the home, in 1966, 275 deaths occurred from poisoning. I say that is 275 too many. I suggest that if parliament has to give approval every time a substance that is determined to be hazardous is put on the schedule of a bill, then while the bill is waiting to be dealt with along with all of the other bills before the house, accidents involving the use of this substance will occur and prove to be fatal.
I was appalled to learn that the banking and commerce committee of the other place that inserted what I consider to be a piece of dangerous red tape in the first draft of the bill did so by a vote of nine to three, thus taking from the minister the power to determine what are hazardous substances and to place them on the schedule. While there may be some amendments moved in regard to various safeguards, in regard to the appeals machinery and so on, I hope very much before the house is through with this measure the provision to which I refer will be eliminated in one way or another. This will restore to the minister the power he should have through this legislation to protect the consumers of this country against hazardous substances.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak briefly on this bill and to support the minister. May I congratulate him on his creditable performance and the leadership he has given since he assumed his portfolio last summer.
This bill, as hon. members are aware, is very similar to Bill S-22 which was previously introduced in the other place, passed there and placed on our order paper, but which with the prorogation of the 27th parliament died on the order paper. We are making progress in this house, though I am not suggesting that we ought to have more elections or prorogations.
I should like to recall a rather amusing book with the title "Mr. Blandings builds his Dream House". According to the book, the only way to build a perfect house was to build one, tear it down and then build another. In the same way, the reconsideration of this bill makes for refinement. As a result, I feel that Bill S-26 is better legislation than was Bill S-22. At the time Bill S-22 was introduced, there was no active Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs headed by the present minister. Aside from the subsequent hazard of substance, the other bill also dealt with another matter, the question of the advertising and sale of contraceptive devices. This part of the legislation should be under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
We have had a very commendable record in this country in ensuring purity and safety of food and drugs under our Food and Drug Directorate. However, there have been a great many products, and new products are arriving daily on the market, which cannot be classified as either food or drugs but at the same time are very important in the evei'y day life of the consumer. In this respect, the legislation currently being introduced by the minister, covers matters that are important to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. In the eyes of the consumer, we have been far behind our neighbours to the south and other countries of the world in providing legislation for the protection of the consumer.
I would like to refer, Mr. Speaker, to one particular section of this bill, namely the one covering poisons. Of 11,000 fatal accidents recorded for the year 1966, a little over 2,000 occurred in the home. I will not go into the details. As an hon. member previously mentioned, 275 of these resulted from poisoning.

With 20 million people in our country, 275 is not a large number, but this bill will be important if even only one life is saved. There were actually over 400 accidental poisonings in the year 1966, 30 per cent of which occurred outside the home.
I would refer to the statistical evidence on poisoning accidents, every one of which could be a fatal accident. This evidence indicates 70 per cent of these accidents involved children under the age of five years. The very high incidence of drug and non-drug poisoning involving very young children points out the urgent necessity for control in this area. It is impossible to prevent every poisoning, but what is required is more awareness by parents and the general public; better labelling, improved packaging and other safety measures in order to reduce accidents to both adults and children and the potential serious injury or loss of life.
Schedule 1 of the bill is very specific. Schedule 2 is rather general in character covering many household cleaners, bleaches and solvents presently used in the home. There are many other hazardous substances in addition to the ones specified. We cannot, of course, know in advance what products will arrive on the market in the future or to what extent they will be hazardous. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) or his colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) must be in a position to act by order in council to add or delete possible classes in schedule 1 and provide reasonable controls for the type of product included in schedule 2, subject of course to the other provisions of the legislation. I am very pleased to support this bill, Mr. Speaker, which is an important step forward in protection of the Canadian people.
